notes.text: Mention — Here begins a new matter, which contains the prophet's prayer, to the end of chap. 64, wherein he begins with mentioning the great kindnesses that God had shewn the Jews, and that emphatically, setting them forth with the greatest advantages.
He said — When he made a covenant with our fathers, and brought them out of Egypt. Not lie - That will keep my covenant. So he - Not Cyrus, Zerubbabel, or Nehemiah, but Christ himself.

The angel — The same that conducted them through the wilderness; the Lord Jesus Christ, who appeared to Moses in the bush. Saved them - From the house of bondage. Carried - He carried them in the arms of his power, and on the wings of his providence. And he is said to do it of old, To remember his ancient kindness for many generations past.

glossa.text: *Of the mercies.* ((HIER.)) The prophet in the person of the Jewish people repenting and acknowledging the mercy of the Lord.

*He was not afflicted.* ((ID.)) The voice which is, etc., *as far as there is no helper but Michael your prince, who stands for the sons of my people ((Dan. X))* .

*And an angel.* ((ID.)) The Septuagint. Not a legate nor an angel himself, but the Lord saved them.

notes.text: Heavens of heavens — Ye highest heavens, the place of God's throne. Waters - Ye clouds which are above a part of the heavens.
Established — He hath made them constant and incorruptible, not changeable, as the things of the lower world. A decree - Concerning their continuance.
Dragons — Either serpents, which hide in the deep caverns of the earth; or whales, and other sea-monsters, which dwell in the depths of the sea.

Fire — Lightnings and other fireworks of the air. Vapor - Or, fumes: hot exhalations. Fulfilling his word - Executing his commands, either for the comfort or punishment of the inhabitants of the earth.
Above — Above all the glories which are in earth and in heaven.

The horn — In scripture commonly denotes strength, victory, glory, and felicity. An exhortation to praise God for his love to his people, ver. 1-5. And for enabling them to overcome their enemies, ver. 6- 9.

glossa.text: *Praise ye the Lord from the heavens.* ((CASS.)) By the mention of a few he exhorts the whole creation to praise God. There are certain things which have a spirit of praising God in that affection wherewith God pleases them: certain have no understanding, but because they themselves are good in their own order, and are referred to the beauty of the whole, they praise not of themselves, but by them God is praised through those that consider them: and so after a sort they praise, because from them the praise of God is born in us, whereto the prophet here admonishes us.

*For he spoke, and they were made.* ((CASS.)) This against those who say that the world is coeternal with God; there follows: *He commanded.* By his word, and they were created. First he said, *made,* afterward *created.* For make we also can, but not create. He therefore alone creates, which is proper to the Godhead. Praise from his works

*He hath established.* From his power he is almighty, whose works are not changed.

*Unto the age, and unto the age of the age.* ((CAS.)) And though the heaven be new, yet they are said to be well established by God, which are made new through Christ and remain bettered. And here is praise from his power.

*Praise ye the Lady *Dominam*; read *Dominum*, "the Lord".* The second part, where, the heavenly things being enumerated, he descends to earthly things. Turning therefore to them, as exhorting us that by the consideration of them we may praise God, which things considered lay open the praise of God, he says: O ye that are of the earth. *All ye deeps.* *ubyssi* ((AUG.)) The depth of the waters, etc., *as far as* these therefore, that is, he exhorts us to praise by the consideration of them.

*Which do his word.* This therefore because it seemed to certain men that God ruled the higher things, but despised these lower ones, and that they were ruled by chance; but these also God does, and in these least things he is praised, and alleluia is sung.

*Confession.* ((CAS.)) Above he spoke first of heaven, afterward of earth; here of all together. And he takes by heaven all higher things, and by earth all lower things. ((AUG.)) *His confession above heaven and earth.* All things confess him in themselves or in others; the beauty of all things is the voice of them that confess, in those who consider them, that is, let those who consider praise him, both from earthly and from heavenly things, than which there is nothing better.
*He hath exalted the horn of his people.* ((ID.)) Behold what Aggeus and Zacharias prophesied. Now the horn of his people is lowly in tribulations, but when the Lord shall come, it shall be exalted.

notes.text:
In this verse the apostle expresses, in his own words, what he expressed before in those of the Psalmist. It became him — It was suitable to all his attributes, both to his justice, goodness, and wisdom. For whom - As their ultimate end. And by whom - As their first cause. Are all things, in bringing many adopted sons to glory - To this very thing, that they are sons, and are treated as such To perfect the captain - Prince, leader, and author of their salvation, by his atoning sufferings for them. To perfect or consummate implies the bringing him to a full and glorious end of all his troubles, chap. v, 9. This consummation by sufferings intimates,

1. the glory of Christ, to whom, being consummated, all things are made subject.

2. The preceding sufferings. Of these he treats expressly, ver. 11- 18; having before spoken of his glory, both to give an edge to his exhortation, and to remove the scandal of sufferings and death. A fuller consideration of both these points he interweaves with the following discourse on his priesthood. But what is here said of our Lord's being made perfect through sufferings, has no relation to our being saved or sanctified by sufferings. Even he himself was perfect, as God and as man, before ever be suffered. By his sufferings, in his life and death, he was made a perfect or complete sin-offering. But unless we were to be made the same sacrifice, and to atone for sin, what is said of him in this respect is as much out of our sphere as his ascension into heaven. It is his atonement, and his Spirit carrying on "the work of faith with power" in our hearts, that alone can sanctify us. Various afflictions indeed may be made subservient to this; and so far as they are blessed to the weaning us from sin, and causing our affections to be set on things above, so far they do indirectly help on our sanctification.

For — They are nearly related to each other. He that sanctifieth - Christ, chap. xiii, 12. And all they that are sanctified - That are brought to God; that draw near or come to him, which are synonymous terms. Are all of one - Partakers of one nature, from one parent, Adam.

I will declare thy name to my brethren -- Christ declares the name of God, gracious and merciful, plenteous in goodness and truth, to all who believe, that they also may praise him. In the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee — As the precentor of the choir. This he did literally, in the midst of his apostles, on the night before his passion. And as it means, in a more general sense, setting forth the praise of God, he has done it in the church by his word and his Spirit; he still does, and will do it throughout all generations. Psalm xxii, 22.

And again — As one that has communion with his brethren in sufferings, as well as in nature, he says, I will put my trust in him - To carry me through them all. And again - With a like acknowledgment of his near relation to them, as younger brethren, who were yet but in their childhood, he presents all believers to God, saying, Behold I and the children whom thou hast given me. Isaiah viii, 17, 18

Since then these children partake of flesh and blood — Of human nature with all its infirmities. He also in like manner took part of the same; that through his own death he might destroy the tyranny of him that had, by God's permission, the power of death with regard to the ungodly. Death is the devil's servant and serjeant, delivering to him those whom he seizes in sin. That is, the devil - The power was manifest to all; but who exerted it, they saw not.

And deliver them, as many as through fear of death were all their lifetime, till then, subject to bondage — Every man who fears death is subject to bondage; is in a slavish, uncomfortable state. And every man fears death, more or less, who knows not Christ: death is unwelcome to him, if he knows what death is. But he delivers all true believers from this bondage.

For verily he taketh not hold of angels — He does not take their nature upon him. But he taketh hold of the seed of Abraham - He takes human nature upon him. St. Paul says the seed of Abraham, rather than the seed of Adam, because to Abraham was the promise made.

Wherefore it behoved him — It was highly fit and proper, yea, necessary, in order to his design of redeeming them. To be made in all things - That essentially pertain to human nature, and in all sufferings and temptations. Like his brethren -- this is a recapitulation of all that goes before: the sum of all that follows is added immediately. That he might be a merciful and faithful High Priest-Merciful toward sinners; faithful toward God. A priest or high priest is one who has a right of approaching God, and of bringing others to him. Faithful is treated of, chap. iii, 2, &c., with its use; merciful, chap. iv, 14, &c., with the use also; High Priest, chap. v, 4, &c., chap. vii, 1, &c. The use is added from chap. x, 19. In things pertaining to God, to expiate the sins of the people - Offering up their sacrifices and prayers to God; deriving God's grace, peace, and blessings upon them.
For in that he hath suffered being tempted himself he is able to succor them that are tempted — That is, he has given a manifest, demonstrative proof that he is able so to do.

glossa.text:
*The author.* Christ. *Of their salvation,* that is, of the sons. For he is son by nature, whose heirs we shall be, we who are sons by adoption. See how great he is in the midst of us: both he is a son, and we are sons. But there is a difference, in that he saves, we are saved. He sanctifies, we are sanctified. Now Scripture joins us together, now it puts us apart. *Many,* he says, *sons,* here it joined together: *the author of their salvation,* here it distinguished. *Through his passion.* Because unless Christ died, man would not be redeemed, and unredeemed would perish. And if that were so, all things would have been made in vain. For the rest serve man, man God. Nor would God be glorified in any, since all things were made for this. The predestination concerning the sons to be brought in would also be false. *To perfect.* This he began in the resurrection, when he was exalted with the glory of immortality. And it was increased in the ascension, when he ascended to the right hand of the Father. And it shall be completed in the judgment, *when all things shall be subjected to him, and he shall be all in all ((I Cor. XV))*. 

*For he,* etc. ((AUG.)) He proves that it was fitting that Christ should suffer for our deliverance, etc., *as far as* since it is agreed that he knew both natures through himself.

*All of one.* But he as the proper Son, we as adopted. When he says: *he is not ashamed to call them brethren,* he shows that our brotherhood is not to him of nature, but of mercy. Which he proves by the prophet, lest it be thought new.

*Because therefore.* As if: Since all were of one, and because the children who were to be sanctified had communicated in flesh, that is, were men of soul and body, which is taken by the blood, corruptible; therefore *he also,* Christ. *He partook of the same,* namely the children, or *of the same,* that is, of flesh and blood, and this in like manner, that is, passible and mortal, that he might be able to die, and so destroy the devil, and through death make void the law, and by grace make free the Jews who through fear of punishments were slaves of the law. *Through death.* A marvel, what? Death was the arms whereby the devil conquered, and by it the devil was conquered by Christ.

*Nowhere.* He partook of the same that he might sanctify men. And rightly is this cause added, because if he were not to deliver them, he would not partake with them. Which appears in the angels, because nowhere, that is, in no scripture, is he read to have taken hold of angels. *He taketh hold.* The Apostle said: *he taketh hold,* and not *he took up,* as if: He overtook one fleeing far off. In which the dignity of human nature can be understood, and the mercy and grace wherewith he did this, and the care which he had for us. For human nature fleeing before him, and fleeing far off (for we were far off); pursuing he took hold of it, not to the angelic, but to human nature was this dignity given, that God should be joined to it in one person.
*In all things.* Because he was born, brought up, he grew; he suffered, he died. He who above was called the figure of the Father's substance.

*For in that.* That is, in the flesh which he took he suffered many cruel things. And he knows by experience what that tribulation of those who suffer is. *Who are tempted.* God tempts that he may prove, the devil that he may deceive, man that he may know what he knows not.

notes.text: That it might be fulfilled — That is, whereby was fulfilled. The original word frequently signifies, not the design of an action, but barely the consequence or event of it. Which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet - on another occasion: Out of Egypt have I called my Son - which was now fulfilled as it were anew; Christ being in a far higher sense the Son of God than Israel, of whom the words were originally spoken. Hosea xi, 1.

Then Herod, seeing that he was deluded by the wise men — So did his pride teach him to regard this action, as if it were intended to expose him to the derision of his subjects. Sending forth - a party of soldiers: In all the confines thereof - In all the neighbouring places, of which Rama was one.

Then was fulfilled — A passage of Scripture, whether prophetic, historical, or poetical, is in the language of the New Testament fulfilled, when an event happens to which it may with great propriety be accommodated.

Rachel weeping for her children — The Benjamites, who inhabited Rama, sprung from her. She was buried near this place; and is here beautifully represented risen, as it were out of her grave, and bewailing her lost children. Because they are not - that is, are dead. The preservation of Jesus from this destruction, may be considered as a figure of God's care over his children in their greatest danger. God does not often, as he easily could, cut off their persecutors at a stroke. But he provides a hiding place for his people, and by methods not less effectual, though less pompous, preserves them from being swept away, even when the enemy comes in like a flood. Jer. xxxi, 15.
He was afraid to go thither — into Judea; and so turned aside into the region of Galilee - a part of the land of Israel not under the jurisdiction of Archelaus.

He came and dwelt in Nazareth — (where he had dwelt before he went to Bethlehem) a place contemptible to a proverb. So that hereby was fulfilled what has been spoken in effect by several of the prophets, (though by none of them in express words, ) He shall be called a Nazarene - that is, he shall be despised and rejected, shall be a mark of public contempt and reproach.

glossa.text: *Take the child,* etc. ((HILAR.)) When he was signifying that she was espoused to a just man, he called her wife; but after the birth she is shown only as the mother of Jesus, so that, as to the just Joseph the marriage with Mary was reckoned in virginity, so her venerable virginity as a mother might be shown in Jesus.

*Who rising up.* Joseph is a figure of the preachers, who bore Christ, with his mother, that is, the faith of Christ and of the Church, to the Gentiles, Herod being left behind, that is, the unbelief of the Jews. *By night.* Because secretly by flight he went down to enlighten Egypt, night being left to the Jews.

By night he bore him into Egypt, because in the night of ignorance he left them to those unbelieving ones from whom he himself withdrew. When he returns, no mention is made of night, because at the end of the world the Jews, receiving the faith as though Christ returning from Egypt, shall be enlightened.

*Into Egypt, and he was there,* etc. He shows [Egypt] venerating a God of every kind: because Christ, not received by the Jews, passes over by preaching to the Gentiles. He fled into Egypt as he was born, that he might repair corrupted nature. So he fled, that he might call back the fugitives. That he fled was a matter of sacrament, not of fear, that he might give his own an example of fleeing. He did not flee death, who had come to die: nor did he dread the snares, who had come to lay open the craft of the devil. Of this flight Isaiah foretold: *Behold the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud,* that is, flesh without sin: *and shall enter into Egypt ((Isa. XIX))*. But for seven years he lay hid in Egypt.

*Out of Egypt I have called.* This is found in Osee according to the Hebrew verity: or in the book of Numbers, as some assert: because the whole was done by the disposition of God.

*Then Herod seeing.* It is likely that, since nothing had been reported to Herod by the Magi, he believed that they had been deceived by a false star, and had therefore not returned to him: whence also he rested so long from the search for the child. Then, when the things which had been done or said in the temple were made public, he perceived that he had been mocked by the Magi, and hastening to the death of Christ he slew the children.

It is likely that for a year and four days from the nativity of Christ Herod raged against the children: which perhaps he deferred for this reason, that he set out for Rome, or was accused there, or that he might consult the Romans concerning those things which were said about Christ. Perhaps therefore he held himself back so long from the search for the child, that he might apprehend him the more carefully, and that he might not be able to slip away in any manner.

*He slew all the children.* As soon as Christ appeared to the world, persecution began against him: which prefigured the persecution of the saints: and while the infant is sought, infants are slain; in whom the form of martyrdom is born, where the infancy of the Church is consecrated.

The death of the little ones figures the passion of all the martyrs, who were slain as little ones, humble and innocent: who suffered not in Judaea only, but everywhere at the hands of the wicked, whom Herod signifies. That they were two years old: because they were perfect in doctrine and in work. Those being slain, Christ escaped: because bodies can be destroyed, the divinity cannot be touched.


*And in all the borders thereof.* He was not content with the devastation of Bethlehem, but laid waste the neighbouring places; nor had he any mercy for age, from a son of one night to a son of two years, but that he slew them all.

*From two years old.* Therefore from two years old, that as Herod had taken in beforehand the borders of the city, so also he might take in beforehand another year. Therefore also from two years old: because he feared lest the child, whom the stars served, should fashion for himself an appearance a little above or below his age.

[0077A]

*Then was fulfilled.* It is called fulfilled: because before it came to pass it was but half-full to those who read it, since what sounded in the letter secretly promised something to come.

((CHRYSOST.)) He says that the star appeared for a year, as in the destruction of the Romans signs appeared in heaven, when the voice of the angels was heard: Let us pass over from these seats.

*A voice in Rama.* That is, in a high place it was spread far and wide.

Allegorically. Or, the voice of the Church groaning over the slaughter of her members ascends to the throne of the judge on high. *A voice in Rama.* On account of the Levite's wife, destroyed by fornication and divided into twelve parts according to the number of the tribes, all Israel destroyed the tribe of Benjamin save three hundred men: the weeping and wailing of those who survived was heard as far as Rama, which is a place near Gabaa, at the twelfth milestone from Bethlehem. *Was heard.* He heightens it, so that hyperbolically Rachel, already dead, is said with the feeling of one grieving to be already weeping for her sons. Whence by this the history concerning the Chaldeans is woven, that the devastation to come from them upon the people of the Jews would be like to the former disaster. But more truly, the Spirit revealing it through the evangelist, the prophecy is taken of the slaughter of the children. He says therefore that what was spoken was then completed, because although the word of the prophecy looks to the impending captivity, yet in it, as in a shadow, the future truth of the slaughter of the infants is proclaimed.

*Rachel.* Because she was buried near Bethlehem, and from the earthly lodging of her body received the name of mother. Or because many of Benjamin and Joseph were slain. Of Rachel was Benjamin born, to whose lot Bethlehem does not belong, but only to the tribe of Judah. But because Judah and Benjamin are neighbouring tribes in the borders of Bethlehem, many also of the tribe of Benjamin were slain.

Note that the figure of the sacrament is better intimated through Rachel (than if Bethlehem were said to have wept), because through her in all things the pattern of the Church is commended, which weeps not so much for those carried off by death as for those destroyed by torment. *Rachel.* That is, the Church, weeps for her tender lambs destroyed: neither will she be comforted in the present, because they are not: but she sends forward all her hope and consolation to the eternal life.

The Church weeps, and will not be comforted here: because her sons are not of this world. Or she weeps: because while she brings forth, she has justice justitiam, whence it is said: *You shall weep,* etc., but a consolation is added: *Your sorrow shall be turned into joy ((Joan. XVI))*.

*But Herod being dead, behold,* etc. Because, the perfidy of the Jews being lulled to sleep, and Elias and Enoch preaching, Judaea shall receive the word of God.

The king being dead, his accomplices straightway perish, so, the persecution of the Church ceasing, she is invited to heavenly things.

*Into the land.* He does not determine into what part, so that, Joseph doubting, the angel may return: and that by his frequent address Joseph may be made the more certain. Because he did not distinguish into what part, therefore Josephus understood Judaea, which was the worthier part of the kingdom. *They are dead.* Some relate that Herod caused the nobler of the Jews to be slain over his own funeral, that he might so compel the Jews to weep for his death.

*Who rising up.* Allegorically. Joseph bears the figure of the apostles, by whose office Christ is carried about. The apostles came first into the land of Israel: because they preached first to the Jews. But because of Herod, that is, the hereditary unbelief remaining, they fear and withdraw, being admonished to preach grace to the Gentiles, and to carry Christ over to them.

The land of Israel being named, it seemed to Joseph that such a child ought to dwell nowhere but in Jerusalem, where the temple was and the celebration of the prophets. Yet the angel wished Galilee to be understood, which the Jews also inhabited, which shows that it had thus been predestined, because he shall be called a Nazarene.

*He feared to go thither.* If he feared Judaea on account of Archelaus, the heir of his father's cruelty, why not Galilee also, where another Herod, his brother, was reigning? Because Archelaus after his father obtained the sole rule of the whole kingdom: but growing insolent he was cast down by Tiberius Caesar into exile at Lyons, and then the kingdom was divided into four tetrarchies, one of which, that is Galilee, Herod his brother obtained.

It is asked: why did Joseph not fear to go into Galilee as into Judaea, since Archelaus reigned there also? But he could better lie hid in Nazareth (which was remote) than in Jerusalem, where was the head of the kingdom and Archelaus constantly present.

*He withdrew into the parts.* That Christ is not carried over thither where Archelaus was reigning signifies that Christ shall be hidden from those in whom Antichrist shall reign.

*Nazareth.* Nazareth is interpreted *a new shoot* or *the flower of the field*, from the root of which shoot the holy of holies is read to have ascended, to signify the substance of his eternity. As therefore he chose the time in which he should be born and the place, so also the city in which he should grow up: whose name is a token that he who is holiness itself, nurtured in holiness, is rightly called the holy of holies: whence also his disciples were first called Nazaraeans, but afterwards from Christ were called Christians.

Nazareth of Galilee, whither he is carried over, signifies that part of the same nation which was to receive the faith: whence it is interpreted *a flower*: because the more ardently the Church passes over from earthly things to heavenly, the more it abounds in the flower and shoot of the virtues.

*By the prophets.* He says prophets in the plural, because we have no fixed instance from Scripture: he shows that he took the sense, not the words. Or in the same words in Isaiah according to the Hebrew verity: *A Nazarene shall ascend from his root ((Isa. XI))*.

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: From the great psalm of the righteous sufferer (Ps 22, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me’). The vindicated one calls the redeemed ‘brothers’ — the citation grounds the solidarity Hebrews needs between the Son and the ‘many children.’

echoes.text: Behold, I and the children whom Yahweh has given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from Yahweh of Armies, who dwells in Mount Zion.
echoes.note: Quoted immediately after 8:17 from the same breath of Isaiah. The prophet's ‘children’ become the Son's ‘children’ — Isaiah's household read as a figure of the redeemed gathered around Christ.

echoes.text: I will wait for Yahweh, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him.
echoes.note: ‘I will put my trust in him’ follows the Greek of Isa 8:17; the same clause appears at 2 Sam 22:3 and Isa 12:2 LXX, so the exact source is debated. Volume is low (one clause), but its pairing with the next line from the same Isaiah passage tips the identification toward Isa 8.

echoes.text: Behold, God is my salvation. I will trust, and will not be afraid; for Yah, Yahweh, is my strength and song; and he has become my salvation.”
echoes.note: Listed as the competing source for ‘I will put my trust in him’: Isa 12:2 LXX reads pepoithōs esomai ep' autō, verbally even closer than Isa 8:17. Beale & Carson treat it as the likeliest single donor, so it is heard here as a low-volume alternate behind the same clause. Contested precisely because Hebrews seems to have conflated the Isaianic ‘trust’ texts.
echoes.altSource: Isaiah 8:17 (printed above as the primary identification)

echoes.text:
Of you comes my praise in the great assembly.
I will pay my vows before those who fear him.
echoes.note: A faint recurrence echo: having quoted Ps 22:22, the author's ‘in the congregation I will sing your praise’ keeps sounding the same psalm's assembly-of-praise language (Ps 22:25, ‘praise in the great assembly’). Low verbal volume beyond the shared ‘assembly/praise,’ but Hays' recurrence test favors hearing the wider psalm once it has been opened.

echoes.text: But let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is of disservice to us, and is contrary to our works, and upbraids us with sins against the law... But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will touch them. (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12; 3:1)
echoes.note: Several scholars (noted in Beale & Carson) hear the Wisdom-of-Solomon portrait of the righteous sufferer, perfected and numbered among God's ‘sons,’ behind Heb 2:10's ‘author of their salvation perfect through sufferings’ bringing ‘many sons to glory.’ Thematic coherence is strong; verbal volume is low and the source is deuterocanonical, hence low confidence.

echoes.text: He shall sprinkle of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it, and make it holy from the uncleanness of the children of Israel.
echoes.note: ‘He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified’ (v. 11) anticipates the sanctifying, sin-cleansing high-priestly work that chs. 9–10 ground in the Day of Atonement (Lev 16). No verbal volume — a faint forward-pointing figure of the cult the letter will expound, consistent with the seeding pattern Hays calls satisfaction.

echoes.text: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: ‘To make atonement for the sins of the people’ (v. 17) reintroduces the Day of Atonement figure first sounded at 1:3 and expounded in chs 9–10. No quotation — the high-priestly, sacrificial pattern itself is the borrowing (figural). The recurrence is the point: the motif is being seeded before the argument arrives.

echoes.text: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham my friend, You whom I have taken hold of from the ends of the earth, and called from its corners, and said to you, ‘You are my servant, I have chosen you and have not cast you away.’
echoes.note: ‘He gives help to the offspring of Abraham’ (v. 16) echoes Isa 41:8–9, where God ‘takes hold of’ (epilambanomai, the very verb Hebrews uses) the chosen ‘offspring of Abraham’ his servant. The shared rare verb plus the ‘seed of Abraham’ phrase gives real verbal volume; thematic coherence (election, help, servant) is strong, so the allusion is widely heard (Beale & Carson).

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.
echoes.note: ‘Through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil’ (v. 14) is read by many as the protoevangelium fulfilled: the woman's offspring crushing the serpent's head, the serpent being identified with the devil in Second Temple and NT tradition. No verbal volume — a figural/typological link resting on thematic coherence (the seed defeats the death-dealing adversary).

echoes.text: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, and those who are of his portion make trial thereof. (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24)
echoes.note: Wisdom 2:24 is the standard Second Temple text identifying the devil with the bringer of death, exactly the equation Heb 2:14 makes (‘him who had the power of death, that is, the devil’). Beale & Carson cite it for the conceptual background; verbal volume is nil and the source deuterocanonical, hence low confidence and an echo at the level of shared idea.

echoes.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? ‘Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.’
echoes.note: ‘Deliver all of them who through fear of death were… subject to bondage’ (vv. 14–15) faintly sounds Hosea's promise to ransom from ‘the power of death/Sheol.’ The taunt over death's power coheres with Hebrews' deliverance theme (and with 1 Cor 15:55, which quotes it), but verbal volume here is low and the link is contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
echoes.note: Explicit fulfillment formula ('that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet'): 'Out of Egypt I called my son.' Verbatim Volume against the Hebrew (not LXX, which reads 'his children'), maximal rhetorical stress, and dense Thematic Coherence — Jesus as God's Son recapitulates Israel's exodus. Paradigm Matthean formula quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses in Midian, “Go, return into Egypt; for all the men who sought your life are dead.” Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them on a donkey, and he returned to the land of Egypt. Moses took God’s rod in his hand. Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go. You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus […]
echoes.note: Moses-typology: God tells Moses 'all who sought your life are dead' (cf. 2:20), Israel is God's 'firstborn son,' and the infant-deliverer is threatened by a murderous king. The flight-into-Egypt / called-out-of-Egypt frame recapitulates the Moses-and-Israel pattern with little verbal borrowing but overwhelming structural coherence; Matthew clearly builds Jesus as a new Moses.

echoes.text: Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well.
echoes.note: Moses flees from Pharaoh who seeks to kill him, paralleling the holy family's flight from Herod who seeks to destroy the child. Herod-as-Pharaoh / Jesus-as-Moses typology; structural rather than verbal, hence figural.

echoes.text: God spoke to Israel in the visions of the night, and said, “Jacob, Jacob!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “I am God, the God of your father. Don’t be afraid to go down into Egypt, for there I will make of you a great nation. I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again. Joseph will close your eyes.”
echoes.note: Israel's family also descends into Egypt for refuge by night under divine reassurance given in a night vision to Jacob ('do not fear to go down to Egypt'). Faint patriarchal recurrence of the protective sojourn-in-Egypt motif undergirding Hosea 11:1; contested.

echoes.text: Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brothers, and they hated him all the more. He said to them, “Please hear this dream which I have dreamed: for behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and also stood upright; and behold, your sheaves came around, and bowed down to my sheaf.” His brothers said to him, “Will you indeed reign over us? Or will you indeed have dominion over us?” They hated him all the more for his […]
echoes.note: Joseph the dreamer leads the family to safety in Egypt; Matthew's Joseph is likewise guided by dreams to and from Egypt. Distinctive shared name + dream-revelation + Egypt motif, but no verbal citation, so low-confidence and contested.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more.
echoes.note: Named formula quotation ('that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled'): 'A voice was heard in Ramah... Rachel weeping for her children... because they are no more.' Verbatim Volume, explicit prophetic attribution, and Thematic Coherence — exile-and-lament now answered by hope (the very chapter promises return), framing the slaughtered innocents within Israel's exile pattern.

echoes.text: Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “You shall cast every son who is born into the river, and every daughter you shall save alive.”
echoes.note: Pharaoh's decree to kill the male Hebrew infants is recapitulated in Herod's massacre of Bethlehem's boys two years and under. Herod-as-Pharaoh typology with strong structural coherence (tyrant slays infants, deliverer escapes); little verbal overlap, hence figural but high confidence given the sustained Moses pattern.

echoes.text: Rachel died, and was buried on the way to Ephrath (the same is Bethlehem).
echoes.note: Rachel dies and is buried 'on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)' — anchoring the weeping mother to the Bethlehem locale of the massacre and explaining why Matthew reaches for the Rachel lament here. Moderate coherence via the geographic tie that activates Jeremiah 31:15.

echoes.text: A man of the house of Levi went and took a daughter of Levi as his wife. The woman conceived, and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months. When she could no longer hide him, she took a papyrus basket for him, and coated it with tar and with pitch. She put the child in it, and laid it in the reeds by the river’s bank. His sister stood far off, to see what would be done to him. Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe at the […]
echoes.note: The infant Moses survives the slaughter of the Hebrew children, prefiguring the threatened-but-preserved child Jesus. Faint, mediated by the broader Pharaoh/Herod pattern; contested as a discrete echo within this pericope.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses in Midian, “Go, return into Egypt; for all the men who sought your life are dead.”
echoes.note: The angel's words 'those who sought the young child's life are dead' (2:20) closely echo the Lord's words to Moses in Midian: 'all the men who sought your life are dead.' Distinctive, near-verbal parallel completing the Moses-return typology; high Volume and high Thematic Coherence even without a formula.

echoes.text: for, behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb: and he shall begin to save Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.”
echoes.note: For 'He will be called a Nazarene,' a leading candidate is the Nazirite consecration of Samson — 'the child shall be a Nazirite (nazir) to God from the womb' — a divinely set-apart deliverer-from-birth. Matthew's plural 'prophets' and the absence of an exact verse suggest a wordplay-cluster; Volume is via sound-alike (Nazoraios/nazir), coherence high. Editorially contested among Nazirite, Branch (netzer), and Nazareth-place readings.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: The other principal candidate for 'He will be called a Nazarene': the Davidic 'branch' (netzer) springing from Jesse's root. The Hebrew netzer gives a strong consonantal pun on Nazoraios/Nazareth and fits the messianic-shoot theme; explains Matthew's vague 'prophets.' Contested against the Nazirite (Judges 13:5) reading; listed as alt of that entry and here in its own right.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will raise to David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.
echoes.note: Parallel 'righteous Branch' (tsemach) messianic-shoot prophecy reinforcing the netzer/Nazarene wordplay field behind 2:23. Faint, mediated, and overlapping Isaiah 11:1; contested.

echoes.text: and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple;
echoes.note: 'Behold, the man whose name is the Branch' — another shoot/Branch text feeding the messianic 'Nazarene' pun cluster Matthew gestures toward with the plural 'prophets.' Low Volume, thematic only; contested.

harmony.title: The Magi and the flight to Egypt
harmony.note: Only Matthew gives the wise men, the star, Herod's fury, and the slaughter of the innocents.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Praise the Lord from the heights; praise him, all you stars.
Let all creation sing.
The child who shares our flesh and blood is here.
He carries us as he was carried.
Even into Egypt, even through the night.
God goes with the ones who flee.
Come, let us worship the God who shares our days.
Thanks be to God. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Praise him from the heights, sun and moon and shining stars — and praise him, too, down here, where a family bundles a child and runs for the border in the dark.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
This is the God who lifts us up and carries us, the way that mother carried her son all the long road into Egypt.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
He took on our flesh and blood, our hunger and our fear, so that he could stand beside us when we are tested.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
So bring your griefs and your gladness alike; the One who shared our days has not let go of us.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Praise God from the heights, all you shining stars.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
He shares our flesh and blood, our fear, our road.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
Even into Egypt, God goes with the child.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us.
Come, let us worship the God who shares our days.
The Word became flesh and dwells among us. Thanks be to God!
